text: The command defaults -currentHost write -g AppleFontSmoothing -int 0 writes one integer into the Mac's global preferences. The -g flag names the global domain every app reads, and -currentHost files the value under the machine's hardware UUID in ~/Library/Preferences/ByHost/, where the old System Preferences checkbox kept it. AppKit reads the key when an app launches, so apps that are already open keep their old text until they are quit and reopened.
title: aadhar.sh: font smoothing

text: The AppleFontSmoothing values date from Mac OS X Snow Leopard, which cut the Appearance pane down to one checkbox. A Terminal command became the only way back to the old menu: 1 for light, 2 for medium and 3 for strong LCD smoothing. On macOS 27.2, a sweep of four fonts (Helvetica, the system font, Tahoma, Verdana), three sizes (11, 13, 16 pt), two backing scales and two polarities found that 1, 2 and 3 render byte-identical bitmaps in all 48 cases. Only 0 differs, so the key works as an on/off switch.
title: aadhar.sh: font smoothing

text: With font smoothing on, macOS AppKit grows every glyph outline before filling it, so each stem widens on both edges. A Helvetica lowercase l at 13 pt on a 1x screen measured 1.14 px wide at 0 and 1.30 px with smoothing on. The growth scales with pixels per em, about 0.0116 px per ppem for dark text on a light background, and stops at 0.6 px. Light text on a dark background grows about 2.75 times faster, 0.032 px per ppem, so the same 13 pt stem reaches 1.55 px in dark mode, 36% heavier than at 0.
title: aadhar.sh: font smoothing

text: Greyscale antialiasing shades each edge pixel by the fraction of it the letter covers and gives all three color channels the same value, so text can be composited over any background. Subpixel rendering treats each LCD pixel as three vertical stripes, red, green and blue, and computes coverage for each stripe, tripling horizontal resolution. The cost is color fringing, which a filter such as FreeType's five-tap LCD filter reduces by spreading each third of a pixel into its neighbours.
title: aadhar.sh: font smoothing

text: macOS Mojave (10.14, 2018) turned off subpixel antialiasing. Subpixel coverage needs three alpha values, one per stripe, so the renderer must know the color behind each glyph when it rasterizes; a GPU-composited, translucent, animated desktop does not know that color yet. An ex-macOS engineer on Hacker News also cited pixel geometry threaded through every graphics layer, glyph caches multiplied by subpixel offsets, and artifacts when text switches between static and animated. Rotated panels and OLEDs without RGB stripes break the three-stripe assumption. Mojave's checkbox became Use font smoothing when available and controlled only the stem thickening; Big Sur removed the checkbox, leaving the defaults key.
title: aadhar.sh: font smoothing

text: Windows made the opposite choices. ClearType is Microsoft's subpixel rendering and has been the Windows system default since Vista; Windows XP shipped with greyscale smoothing as the default, like Windows 2000. Windows fonts rely on hinting, instructions inside the font that move outlines onto the pixel grid before rasterizing, so a stem snaps to whole pixel columns. Joel Spolsky described the split in 2007: Apple preserves the typeface's shape at the cost of blur, Microsoft fits letters to pixel boundaries at the cost of fidelity. DirectWrite later added fractional glyph positioning, and modern Windows UI text renders in greyscale.
title: aadhar.sh: font smoothing

text: Text on a Mac looks worse than on Windows on common external monitors because macOS tunes rendering for about 220 PPI while 24- and 27-inch 1080p and 1440p monitors sit between 92 and 109 PPI. At 1x, macOS draws with no subpixel rendering and no hinting, so a 1.14 px stem straddles two pixel columns as two greys, and smoothing adds 0.15 px (0.41 px in dark mode). A 27-inch 4K monitor set to look like 2560x1440 is drawn at 5120x2880 and then scaled by 0.75 to 3840x2160, filtering every glyph a second time. Panels where 2x lands exactly on native, such as 5K at 27 inches and 6K at 32 inches, avoid both problems.
title: aadhar.sh: font smoothing

text: Setting AppleFontSmoothing to 0 on a 1x monitor removes about 13% of extra stem width for black-on-white text and 36% for white-on-black, making text lighter but still soft; it cannot restore subpixel rendering or hinting. On Retina screens the choice is mostly taste. In CSS, -webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased requests the unthickened rendering for an element in Safari and Chrome on macOS. With the system set to 0, subpixel-antialiased was measured drawing the same pixels as antialiased in both Chrome and WebKit, so CSS can turn the thickening off but cannot turn it back on.
title: aadhar.sh: font smoothing

text: Turning AppleFontSmoothing off barely affects performance. The stem thickening happens when a glyph is rasterized, before it is stored in the glyph cache. Timing AppKit drawing a 33-character Helvetica line 3,000 times on macOS 27.2: at 3,000 distinct sizes, where every glyph is rasterized fresh, smoothing 0 took 380 to 397 ms and smoothing on took 464 to 473 ms, about 20% more (repeat runs at 0 differed by 17 ms). Drawing the same 13 pt line 3,000 times took 41 to 44 ms at either setting, because cached glyphs cost the same. The extra cost is roughly a microsecond per glyph, paid once per glyph and size.
title: aadhar.sh: font smoothing

text: AppleFontSmoothing 0 is not the same as turning antialiasing off. At 0, macOS still antialiases text in greyscale and only skips the stem thickening: one 13 pt Helvetica line used 224 distinct grey levels at 0 and 229 with smoothing on. With antialiasing switched off in the graphics context, the same line used 2 levels, pure black and white, and the smoothing value no longer changed any pixel. The old Appearance pane's 'Turn off text smoothing for font sizes N and smaller' option, stored as AppleAntiAliasingThreshold, was the real antialiasing switch; on macOS 27.2, setting it to 14 left 13 pt text antialiased in an offscreen render.
title: aadhar.sh: font smoothing
